one_liner: Dependency-free, safe-Rust WHATWG URL parser with Ada's API; faster than ada::url, slower than ada::url_aggregator and can_parse.
what_it_does: A from-scratch WHATWG URL parser in pure Rust (std only, `unsafe_code = "forbid"`) that copies Ada's public interface: `parse::<UrlAggregator>(input, base)` / `parse::<Url>(input, base)`, `can_parse`, Ada-named getters, setters and `has_*` checks, `get_components`, `href_from_file`, and `set_max_input_length`. `UrlAggregator` stores one serialized buffer plus u32 component offsets, so its getters return borrowed `&str`. `Url` has Ada's owned-getter surface. Conformance comes from Ada's pinned WPT fixtures (921 parse cases, 296 setter cases, 2670 of the 2671 IdnaTestV2 cases), which run on every `cargo test`, plus a daily CI job against Ada main.
how_it_is_fast: Several fast paths run before a full parse. The first is a single-pass scanner for already-canonical http(s) URLs. It checks bytes against a 256-entry byte-class bitmask table, ANDing class bits for 8, 4 or 2 bytes at a time, and on success copies the input verbatim into the buffer and records offsets. Further direct paths cover ftp/ws/wss, common normalization (percent-encoding, dot segments, IPv4, IPv6, IDNA) and clean non-special URLs; anything else goes to a spec-literal state machine over a `Vec<char>`, whose result is re-serialized into the aggregator. There is no SIMD (the author dropped the hostname-SWAR and wider-scan-block experiments). The large setter gains come from rewriting only the affected byte range and shifting offsets instead of reparsing.
when_to_use: You need WHATWG-conformant URL parsing in pure safe Rust, with no C++ toolchain, FFI or unsafe code, and want Ada's API shape and Ada-fixture conformance.
Getter-heavy code on `UrlAggregator`: component getters are borrowed slices of one buffer with no allocation.

Code that repeatedly rewrites the query, fragment or credentials of http(s)/ws/ftp URLs: these setters edit a range in place, at ~15 ns for an ASCII query and ~100 ns for a Unicode query on an M4. That is a Lucid before/after gain, not a comparison with Ada.
You are porting code built on Ada's multi-string `ada::url` and parse-plus-href cost matters: Lucid's `Url` took 85.41 vs 108.54 ns/URL. Lucid's own `UrlAggregator` is faster still, at 59.70.
Mostly absolute, canonical http(s) inputs such as crawled or logged URLs, which stay on the fastest scanner path.
when_not_to_use: Top parse or validation throughput: in the project's own run Ada's `url_aggregator` (57.26 vs 59.70 ns/URL) and `can_parse` (11.25 vs 12.95 ns/URL) are faster, and the README says parsing experiments 'did not show a dependable across-the-board gain'.
Hot relative-URL resolution: with a base, every call reparses the base href and runs the char-based state machine, skipping all fast paths. There is no benchmark for this case.

Hot hostname/host/port/pathname/protocol setters: they reparse the whole URL through the generic state machine and rebuild it. Before the range-edit work, query and credential setters on this same path took ~2.5-3.9 µs per call.
You need URLSearchParams, URLPattern, Ada's C API, a crates.io release or semver guarantees: none exist yet. The 0.1.0 release PR is still open.

Binary size or maturity matter: the native object is 45% larger than Ada's (462.1 vs 318.4 KiB, measured against an older Ada pin) because of built-in Unicode/IDNA tables. The repo is ~2 months old with 4 stars, and there is no fuzzing (the fuzz targets are out of scope and not in the tree).

integration.min_toolchain: Rust 1.87 (declared rust-version, edition 2024); CI only tests stable
integration.platforms: any Rust target (pure safe Rust, no arch-specific code); CI tests Linux, macOS and Windows; published performance numbers cover only Apple M4 (aarch64)
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. Both types are plain owned data (a String plus offsets) with no interior mutability. The max-input-length limit is a process-global `AtomicU32` using Relaxed ordering.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — the Rust API reuses Ada's C++ names (parse::<Url|UrlAggregator>, can_parse, get_*/set_*/has_*, get_components) but it is not a C/C++ ABI replacement, it has no url_search_params, URLPattern or ada_c, and `Url` is internally an aggregator, not Ada's multi-string layout

gotchas: `Url` only wraps `UrlAggregator`. Its owned getters (get_href, get_protocol, get_host, get_hostname, get_port, get_search, get_hash) clone into a new String on every call. The headline 1.27x win comes from this layout difference, and `UrlAggregator` is the faster type to use.

Only set_search/set_hash on special non-opaque URLs and set_username/set_password on special non-file URLs are in-place range edits. Every other setter, and those same setters on file, non-special or opaque URLs, reparses the whole buffer.
Setting `set_max_input_length` to anything except the default u32::MAX makes `can_parse` skip every fast path and run a full parse. The setting is global to the process.
The error type has a single `TypeError` variant ('invalid URL'), so it gives no detail on why a parse failed.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Choose it over Ada (C++, or Ada's Rust bindings) only when pure safe Rust with no C++ build is worth ~4% slower aggregator parsing and ~15% slower can_parse. Over sorug, another pure-Rust WHATWG parser that is benchmarked against servo url rather than Ada, choose it when you want Ada's API and Ada's fixture suite; ada-rs publishes a larger lead over C++ Ada, but only on a 9-URL corpus.
verified_claims_summary: The benchmark links Lucid and amalgamated Ada b2c2d7f6 into one Google Benchmark binary and runs Ada's pinned 100,025-URL corpus, taking the mean of 5 reps. Setup: Apple M4, macOS 26.5, Rust 1.98.0 with target-cpu=native against Apple Clang 21 at -O3 -mcpu=native, LTO off on both sides, simdutf off. Result: Lucid `Url` parse+href 85.41 vs `ada::url` 108.54 ns/URL (1.27x); `UrlAggregator` 59.70 vs `ada::url_aggregator` 57.26 (Ada ~4% faster); can_parse 12.95 vs 11.25 (Ada ~15% faster). The raw JSON matches these numbers, shows zero validity or serialization disagreements, and records a 1-minute load average of ~4.5.
status_note: Active (created 2026-07-30, last commit 2026-09-07) and MIT-licensed, but not yet on crates.io, so use it as a git dependency. It is small, dependency-free safe Rust that can be vendored, and a daily CI job tracks Ada main's fixtures.
